construction_adaptations.reason: Keep the real cannon carriage and wheel envelope clear of the forecastle break; authored construction placement, not a recovered retail dimension.

A real continuous head timber above the 0.85m-high gun opening: cannon centre 0.65–0.67m above floor, opening top 1.075–1.095m, leaving at least 0.155m of closed timber below the rail. No disconnected local roof patches.
Move the foremast 0.492m forward on the same forecastle platform so its real trunk clears the aft forecastle bulkhead. Cannon count32, platforms, mast/sail dimensions and common helpers unchanged.

notes: Provision casks and planked storage crates occupy a framed lower hold with main hatch access.
The preserved lower gun deck remains a separate working level with open access from the weather deck and a further descent to the hold.
Plain aft room below the raised sterncastle uses a chart table, seating, bunk and storage furniture; modest glass stern lights are an explicit inferred adaptation.

Hand-worked capstan and pump well, rope stowage, optional carried-boat skids and a removable-pot officer facility are authored period-style adaptations to the large armed game family; they do not establish exact early-caravel equipment.

supports: The museum describes fifteenth-century lateen caravels with two or three masts carrying triangular sails.
evidence.limits: Confirms the rig family. The twentieth-century model is not a surviving caravel and gives no verified POTC interior.

supports: The archive holds a photograph identified as a three-mast lateen caravel model on display.
evidence.limits: Confirms a recognized three-mast interpretation, with no measured internal arrangement.

supports: Boa Esperança is an approximate wooden discovery-era caravel reconstruction with triangular sails.
The historical type is described with one deck and a small sterncastle.
evidence.limits: This is a two-mast modern training replica; its bunks, toilets, kitchen, fuel and other modern safety/comfort equipment are not treated as historical evidence. The larger armed game-family hull and three lateen masts are retained.

supports: The museum identifies provision casks in the hold and a brick-lined cooking hearth forward of the mainmast.
Senior officers lived in aft sterncastle cabins with glass windows and furniture.
evidence.limits: A 1628 warship analogue for construction and room hierarchy only; no claim that a merchant held Vasa-scale decoration or its exact internal arrangement.

supports: The museum lists a hold, powder room, great cabin, bread room, smaller cabins, heads and furniture within its wooden seventeenth-century merchant reconstruction.
The builders consulted Witsen, Van Yk, VOC documents, paintings and wrecks; the museum explicitly acknowledges incomplete evidence for the interior.

evidence.limits: Batavia is a Dutch East Indiaman, not a fluit or the game Pinnace. Use room types and visible timber construction as period analogues; the asset layout remains an authored reconstruction.
